summary: In this episode of the Lord of Spirits, hosts Father Andrew Stephen Damick and Father Stephen DeYoung explore the active ministry of angels and glorified saints in God's kingdom, emphasizing that the age to come is not static but filled with purposeful work. They discuss the twofold ministry of intercession and governance, drawing on scriptural and Second Temple Jewish texts to show that seeking angelic and saintly intercession is a longstanding practice. The hosts address objections to venerating saints and angels, clarifying the distinction between worship (offering sacrifice) and veneration (honor), and they tackle the topic of necromancy, explaining why Orthodox Christian interaction with the departed is not necromancy but communion in Christ. The episode also includes listener questions on mental illness and spiritual affliction, the nature of ruling with Christ, and the possibility of demonic possession for baptized Christians.

concepts.title: Angelic Intercession
concepts.summary: The belief that angels and saints intercede before God on behalf of humans, a practice rooted in Scripture and Second Temple Jewish tradition.

concepts.title: Veneration vs. Worship
concepts.summary: The Orthodox distinction between worship (offering sacrifice to God alone) and veneration (honor given to saints and angels), addressing Protestant objections.

concepts.title: Royal Priesthood
concepts.summary: The concept that glorified humans and angels serve as both kings and priests, ruling and interceding in God's administration, as seen in Revelation 20.

concepts.title: Necromancy vs. Communion with Saints
concepts.summary: The distinction between necromancy (attempting to control the dead for forbidden knowledge) and Orthodox prayer with the departed saints, which is communion in Christ.

claims.text: Angels and saints intercede before God on behalf of humans, as evidenced by Scripture and Second Temple Jewish texts.
True worship consists of offering sacrifice to God alone, while veneration is honor given to saints and angels.
The saints in glory reign with Christ and serve as priests, interceding and offering worship, as described in Revelation 20.
Asking saints to pray for us is not necromancy because it is not an attempt to control the dead for forbidden knowledge, but a communion in Christ.
Demonic possession does not happen accidentally; it requires an invitation, whether explicit or gradual, and can occur even to baptized Christians who apostatize.
